title: Tell wound infection from colonization without a lab
mechanism_check: Infection is bacteria invading tissue and triggering a host response; colonization is bacteria sitting on the surface without invading.
The crossing signs are systemic or spreading: warmth, redness advancing past margins, swelling, pain out of proportion, fever, foul pus.
A wound identical at 48 hours as at hour zero is likely colonized; a wound that looks worse is infected until proven otherwise.
improvised_tools: A pen mark or paper ruler to outline the redness border for comparison.
A thermometer plus a watch: fever with spreading redness settles the question.
Phone-camera photos of the wound edge for daily visual comparison.
steps: Photograph and mark the redness border at the first exam; record pain level and odor.
Recheck at 12 and 24 hours, comparing margin, drainage amount, and pain trend.
Treat as infected when you see spreading redness, rising pain, pus, or fever.
Treat as colonized when the wound is stable or improving, pain-free, and odor-free.
Write the verdict and the reasoning in the chart so the next shift can trust the call.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: a spreading infection outruns field judgment fast, so reach a physician or urgent care when redness advances.
Do not attempt a verdict from a single snapshot; one look cannot separate colonization from early infection.
Stop and escalate for fever above 101.5F with rapid spread, red streaks, or foul gray drainage.

title: Rig a gravity-fed wound irrigation setup from clinic stock
mechanism_check: Irrigation removes debris and bacteria by mechanical force; pressure matters more than volume, and sterile pressure must stay low to avoid driving debris deeper.
Gravity feed from roughly a meter of height delivers the gentle pressure sweet spot without a syringe or pressure device.
Clean potable water or saline both work; the failure mode is dirty water or excessive pressure, not the container.
improvised_tools: A clean IV bag, water bottle, or zip bag hung about one meter above the wound.
Saline if stocked; otherwise boiled-then-cooled potable water.
Tubing, a small puncture in the bag corner, or a clean squeeze bottle to direct flow.
steps: Prepare clean saline or cooled boiled water before touching the wound.
Hang the reservoir about one meter above the wound and direct a steady stream across the surface.
Irrigate from the cleanest edge outward so flow carries debris away from the center.
Continue until runoff runs clear and no visible debris remains.
Cover with a clean dry dressing and note the irrigation in the chart.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: deep puncture wounds, bites, and wounds with embedded material need a clinician before irrigation alone.
Do not attempt high-pressure irrigation on deep wounds; force drives contamination deeper.
Stop if bleeding restarts heavily or tissue planes open under the stream and seek professional care.

title: Assess dehydration without lab values
mechanism_check: Dehydration is fluid leaving faster than it enters; the body sacrifices skin elasticity, saliva, and urine output before core function fails.
Skin turgor, mucous membrane moisture, urine color and volume, and mental status together triangulate severity better than any single sign.
In the elderly, skin turgor is unreliable (age-related elasticity loss); lean on membranes, output, and mental status instead.
improvised_tools: Your pinch test on the forearm or sternum and a 2-second count for recoil.
A tongue depressor or finger to check the tongue and inner cheek for dryness.
A marked bottle or jug to measure urine output over the shift.
steps: Pinch forearm skin, release, and count the seconds until it flattens; check tongue and cheek moisture.
Ask about fluid intake and urine frequency; inspect urine color against a pale target.
Classify: mild (thirst, dark urine), moderate (dry membranes, slow turgor, low output), severe (confusion, no urine, rapid weak pulse).
Start oral rehydration for mild to moderate cases immediately while planning next steps.
Log the exam findings and classification for the next caregiver.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: severe dehydration with confusion, no urine output, or shock signs needs professional care, not just oral fluids.
Do not attempt oral rehydration when the patient cannot swallow safely or is unconscious.
Stop oral fluids and escalate if vomiting persists, confusion worsens, or no urine appears within hours.

title: Build a limb elevation and compression rig from bandages and padding
mechanism_check: Elevation lets gravity drain edema fluid away from the injury; compression narrows tissue space so fluid cannot pool back in.
The rig fails when compression is uneven (creates a tourniquet effect at the tight spots) or elevation is below heart level.
Effective elevation is about 15 to 30 degrees above the heart, sustained, not a brief lift.
improvised_tools: Elastic bandages or torn cloth strips for wrap; cotton padding or folded towels underneath.
Pillows, a backpack, or a box stack to hold the limb above heart level.
Your finger test: skin below the wrap stays warm and pink, and toes or fingers stay mobile.
steps: Pad bony prominences with cotton or folded cloth before any wrap.
Wrap from the far end toward the body with even, overlapping half-turns at moderate tension.
Elevate the limb above heart level on a stable support and keep it there between treatments.
Recheck circulation every 15 minutes at first: warmth, color, sensation, movement.
Loosen immediately and rewrap if numbness, tingling, or pale cool skin appears.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: compartment-syndrome signs (severe pain with stretch, tense swelling) are surgical territory, not wrapping territory.
Do not attempt compression over a suspected fracture or an infected wound without a clinician's order.
Stop the rig if distal pulse fades or numbness appears; remove the wrap and reassess.

title: Close a clean minor wound with adhesive strips when sutures are absent
mechanism_check: Closure works when wound edges meet without tension; adhesive strips hold edges together by surface grip, not by penetrating tissue like sutures.
Strips fail on gaping, curved, or high-tension wounds and on joints that bend constantly.
The window is narrow: closure helps within roughly 6 to 12 hours on clean wounds; older wounds get cleaned and left open under professional guidance.
improvised_tools: Adhesive strips, butterflies, or medical tape cut into narrow strips.
Tincture of benzoin or clean dry skin prep so strips actually stick.
Clean gauze and saline to prepare the wound bed before closing.
steps: Clean and irrigate the wound thoroughly, then dry the surrounding skin completely.
Approximate the edges with your fingers to confirm they meet without tension.
Place strips across the wound at right angles, starting mid-wound, spacing about 3 mm apart.
Support with a light dressing and instruct the patient to keep the area dry.
Inspect daily for infection signs and plan strip removal around day 7 to 10.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: any wound that gapes, is deep, involves a joint or face, or arrived dirty needs professional closure decisions.
Do not attempt closure on puncture wounds, bites, crush injuries, or wounds older than about 12 hours.
Stop and seek professional care at the first sign of infection: spreading redness, pus, fever, or increasing pain.

title: Separate fracture from sprain with mechanism plus exam
mechanism_check: Bone breaks under axial load, direct blow, or torsion; ligaments tear under stretch and twist, so the story of HOW it happened predicts the structure damaged.
Point tenderness directly over bone, deformity, and inability to bear weight point toward fracture; diffuse swelling with preserved bony landmarks leans sprain.
The Ottawa rules are the classic mechanism: ankle fracture risk when the patient cannot bear weight for four steps or has bony tenderness at the malleolus or midfoot.
improvised_tools: A one-finger palpation sweep along the bone to map exact tenderness points.
A 4-step walk test to check weight-bearing ability.
Comparison against the uninjured side for swelling, shape, and range of motion.
steps: Take the mechanism story: fall height, direction of twist, direct blow, sound heard.
Palpate the full bone with one fingertip, marking every point of sharp tenderness.
Test weight bearing for four steps and compare motion to the uninjured side.
Classify high-suspicion (deformity, bony point tenderness, no weight bearing) versus low-suspicion.
Immobilize as if fractured whenever suspicion is high and document findings for the clinician.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: high-suspicion findings mean imaging and a clinician decide, not the field exam.
Do not attempt to realign, straighten, or test the range of a deformed limb.
Stop and immobilize immediately if deformity, numbness, or pale cool skin appears below the injury.

title: Construct a rigid splint from clinic castoffs
mechanism_check: A splint works by spanning the joints above and below the injury so the broken structure cannot move.
Rigidity comes from the splint board, not from tight wrapping; padding protects skin and fills gaps so pressure distributes evenly.
The classic failure is a splint that ends at the injury site, leaving the far joint free to lever the fracture.
improvised_tools: Cardboard, folded magazines, or a wooden board as the rigid layer.
Cloth, towels, or cotton roll as padding between board and skin.
Tape, bandages, or cloth ties to secure without a commercial splint.
steps: Pad the rigid board so no hard edge touches skin directly.
Position the limb as found; never force it straight.
Lay the splint to span one joint above and one joint below the injury.
Secure with three ties (above, below, and at the injury level), snug but not tight.
Recheck circulation beyond the splint every 15 minutes.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: any fracture needs imaging and professional setting once you have immobilized it.
Do not attempt to straighten a deformed limb or reduce a dislocation in the field.
Stop and loosen the ties at once if fingers or toes go numb, pale, or cold.

title: Run an improvised instrument sterilization workflow
mechanism_check: Sterilization kills microbes through heat or chemistry plus time; the enemy is the assumption that a quick rinse equals sterile.
Boiling at a rolling boil kills most pathogens in 20 minutes but does not equal autoclave sterility; it is the honest middle tier when the autoclave is gone.
Dilute bleach disinfects surfaces and non-critical tools; it corrodes fine instruments, so match the method to the tool's job.
improvised_tools: A lidded pot, clean water, and a heat source for the rolling-boil method.
Household bleach diluted to roughly 1:10 for surface and non-critical disinfection.
Clean tongs for handling, plus sun-drying on a clean cloth for the final dry stage.
steps: Scrub instruments clean first; no sterilization method works through organic debris.
Boil heat-tolerant metal instruments at a full rolling boil for 20 minutes, timer on.
Soak non-boilable, non-critical items in 1:10 bleach solution for 10 minutes, then rinse clean.
Handle with clean tongs only and sun-dry or air-dry on a clean cloth.
Label the batch with date and method so the next user knows what tier of clean this is.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: this is emergency-tier reprocessing for non-critical instruments, not a replacement for autoclave sterility on surgical tools.
Do not attempt to reuse anything on invasive or surgical procedures without autoclave-level sterilization.
Stop and discard rather than reprocess if instruments remain visibly soiled after scrubbing.

title: Track vital-sign trends on a paper flowsheet to catch deterioration early
mechanism_check: Deterioration announces itself as a trend long before it becomes a crisis number; a single reading is a snapshot, a series is a story.
The high-yield signals are respiratory rate, pulse, and mental status; temperature and blood pressure confirm but usually lag.
The flowsheet works because it makes the trend visible to any clinician at a glance, regardless of who took the readings.
improvised_tools: Grid paper or a printed flowsheet: time across the top, vitals down the side.
A watch with a second hand for respiratory rate and pulse counts.
A pen in two colors or circled values to flag anything outside the patient's baseline.
steps: Record baseline vitals on arrival: pulse, respiratory rate, mental status, temperature.
Repeat on a fixed schedule (every 15 to 60 minutes by acuity) and plot each value in its row.
Circle any value that worsens two readings in a row or jumps from baseline.
Hand the sheet, not just a verbal summary, to the next caregiver at handoff.
Escalate when the trend worsens even if individual numbers still look borderline normal.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: a worsening trend is your early-warning system firing, so escalate to a physician before the numbers crash.
Do not attempt to reassure yourself with one good reading after three bad ones; the trend rules.
Stop watchful waiting and escalate immediately on new confusion, respiratory rate above 30, or a falling pulse with low pressure.

title: Work up a fever with a limited diagnostic kit
mechanism_check: Fever is the body raising its thermostat to fight infection; the diagnostic question is local source versus systemic illness.
Pattern narrows the field: fever with cough points to lungs, with burning urination to bladder, with stiff neck and headache toward meningitis.
Danger signs are fever plus altered mental status, stiff neck, rash that does not blanch, or breathing difficulty; those end the workup and start the referral.
improvised_tools: A thermometer and a written log: time, temperature, and associated symptoms each round.
A flashlight for throat, ear, and skin inspection.
A simple symptom checklist so nothing gets skipped under pressure.
steps: Log temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate, then examine head to toe with the flashlight.
Ask the focused questions: cough, urinary symptoms, headache, abdominal pain, rashes, recent wounds.
Match findings to a likely source or mark the fever as source-unknown.
Treat the fever with fluids and antipyretics while the source question resolves.
Document pattern and findings for the clinician who takes over.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: fever with confusion, stiff neck, non-blanching rash, or breathing trouble is an emergency referral, not a workup.
Do not attempt to ride out a fever above 104F or one lasting more than three days without a clinician.
Stop the workup and escalate if the patient deteriorates at any point during observation.

title: Write a prolonged-care plan with minimal stock
mechanism_check: Prolonged care is rationing plus rhythm: stretch supplies by scheduling them where they matter most and doing the basics perfectly.
The plan fails without three things: a written schedule, assigned owners, and a resupply or escalation trigger date.
Priorities order themselves: airway and breathing, circulation, fluids, wounds, meds, comfort; everything else is a luxury tier.
improvised_tools: A single-page care schedule: tasks, times, and owner names in a visible spot.
A supply inventory with burn-rate math: what you have divided by daily use.
A written escalation trigger: exactly what condition sends the patient up the chain.
steps: List every active problem and rank it by what kills first.
Assign each problem a scheduled task, an owner, and a supply line on the sheet.
Calculate burn rate per supply and mark the date each critical item runs out.
Write the escalation triggers in plain language the night shift can act on.
Review the plan at each shift handoff and rewrite it when anything changes.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: prolonged care buys time toward professional care, it never replaces the evacuation or referral plan.
Do not attempt prolonged care for conditions beyond your license and training, even with a perfect plan on paper.
Stop and escalate immediately if any trigger fires or if supplies for a life-critical task run out.

title: Set up sharps containment and waste segregation in a pop-up clinic
mechanism_check: Needlestick injuries transmit bloodborne disease; the injury happens in the gap between use and disposal, so disposal must be at arm's reach.
A sharps container works by being puncture-proof, closable, and never overfilled; the container material matters more than its branding.
Waste segregation matters because mixing sharps with soft waste makes every bag a hazard for whoever handles it downstream.
improvised_tools: A rigid plastic bottle or laundry-detergent jug as the sharps vessel: puncture-proof and closable.
Heavy tape to seal the container at the three-quarter mark.
Separate bags or boxes labeled sharps, soft clinical waste, and general trash.
steps: Place a sharps vessel within arm's reach of every spot where needles are used.
Drop needles straight in after use; never recap, bend, or pass them hand to hand.
Seal each vessel with tape when three-quarters full and start a new one.
Sort soft clinical waste into its own labeled bags, away from general trash.
Document the improvised system so the waste team knows what they are handling.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: any needlestick exposure needs professional post-exposure guidance the same day, not just first aid.
Do not attempt to reuse, recap, or fish sharps out of a container for any reason.
Stop and seal any container that overflows, leaks, or cannot close securely.

title: Run an oral rehydration schedule when IV fluids are rationed
mechanism_check: Oral rehydration works through the gut's sodium-glucose pump: sugar plus salt together pull water across the intestinal wall far faster than water alone.
Small frequent sips beat large gulps because a dehydrated gut rejects volume it cannot absorb, triggering vomiting and losing ground.
The schedule is the therapy; random sipping fails while measured dosing on a clock succeeds.
improvised_tools: Clean water with measured salt and sugar, or any pre-mixed ORS packets in stock.
A marked cup or bottle so each dose is measured, not guessed.
A clock and a written dosing log: time, amount offered, amount kept down.
steps: Mix the solution to the correct ratio; too much salt is worse than none.
Offer small measured doses every 5 minutes, increasing as tolerated.
Log every dose with what was kept down versus vomited.
Watch urine output and mental status as your absorption gauges.
Escalate the plan when intake cannot keep pace with losses.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: IV fluids are a clinical decision; oral rehydration is the bridge, and severe cases still need professional care.
Do not attempt oral rehydration in patients who cannot swallow safely or are unconscious.
Stop oral fluids and escalate if vomiting is continuous, confusion worsens, or no urine appears.

title: Recognize red-flag rashes and route them correctly
mechanism_check: Most rashes are benign and self-limited; the dangerous ones announce themselves with blanching failure, blistering, mucosal involvement, or systemic symptoms.
The glass test (pressing a clear tumbler against the rash) separates blanching rashes from purpura, which signals bleeding under the skin.
Fever plus rash plus altered mental status is the triad that ends deliberation and starts urgent referral.
improvised_tools: A clear glass or plastic cup for the blanching test.
A flashlight to inspect the mouth, eyes, and skin folds where rashes hide.
A phone camera for a timestamped record of the rash pattern.
steps: Inspect the full body including mouth, eyes, palms, soles, and skin folds.
Press the glass against the rash: note whether it fades (blanching) or persists.
Check for fever, confusion, breathing difficulty, and blistering.
Route blanching benign-appearing rashes to routine follow-up; route everything else upward.
Photograph and document the pattern for the clinician who takes over.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: a non-blanching rash, blistering with mucosal involvement, or rash with fever and confusion needs urgent professional evaluation.
Do not attempt to diagnose or treat a rash with systemic symptoms as a routine skin issue.
Stop and escalate at once for rapidly spreading rash, facial or airway swelling, or breathing difficulty.

title: Prevent pressure injuries with a two-person turning schedule
mechanism_check: Pressure injuries form when sustained pressure starves tissue of blood; damage starts within hours on heels, sacrum, and shoulder blades.
Relief works by redistributing pressure on a schedule, not by occasional repositioning; the 2-hour turn is the classic rhythm because tissue recovers in the off-load window.
Pillows and angles matter more than strength: a 30-degree tilt unloads the sacrum without the effort of a full roll.
improvised_tools: Pillows, rolled blankets, or folded towels as positioning wedges.
A visible turning schedule on the wall with times and positions.
A skin-inspection flashlight check built into every turn.
steps: Post the schedule: turns every 2 hours, alternating left tilt, right tilt, and back.
Use pillows to hold 30-degree tilts and keep heels floating off the mattress.
Inspect heels, sacrum, elbows, and shoulder blades at every turn.
Log each turn with position and skin findings on the chart.
Adjust the schedule tighter for patients already showing redness.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: broken skin, blistering, or deep tissue injury needs professional wound management, not just turning.
Do not attempt to massage reddened pressure areas; pressure massage damages compromised tissue further.
Stop and escalate if redness fails to fade within 30 minutes of off-loading.

title: Improvise cold therapy for swelling without ice packs
mechanism_check: Cold constricts vessels and slows the inflammatory cascade; the therapy is controlled cooling, not freezing, and the skin is the limiting factor.
The 20-minutes-on rule exists because longer exposure risks cold injury while shorter bursts barely penetrate.
A damp barrier between cold source and skin is what prevents frostnip; the barrier is the safety device, not an accessory.
improvised_tools: Cold water from a tap or well, wet cloths, and a shady spot as the baseline method.
A damp towel between any colder source and the skin, always.
A timer or watch to enforce the 20-minute cycle.
steps: Confirm this is a fresh soft-tissue injury where cold helps, not an open wound.
Wrap the cold source in a damp cloth; never apply a freezing object directly to skin.
Apply for 20 minutes, then remove for at least 20 minutes before repeating.
Elevate the area during cooling for the combined effect.
Stop the cycles and reassess if pain sharply increases or the area goes numb.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: cold therapy manages swelling; it does not diagnose or fix fractures, dislocations, or vascular injuries underneath.
Do not attempt cold therapy on open wounds, frostbite-risk areas, or skin with poor circulation.
Stop immediately and rewarm gently if skin turns white, waxy, or numb.

title: Build a personal differential-diagnosis habit
mechanism_check: Diagnostic error usually comes from anchoring on the first plausible answer, not from lack of knowledge; a forced list of alternatives breaks the anchor.
The mechanism is generation before selection: write three to five possibilities first, then rank by fit, then test the top two against the evidence.
Vindictive mnemonics beat vibes: a structured list (vascular, infectious, traumatic, autoimmune, metabolic) catches what free recall misses.
improvised_tools: A pocket card or phone note with your chosen differential framework.
Three blank lines on every patient note: possibles, ranking, what would disprove each.
A weekly review of one case where your first answer was wrong.
steps: Before examining, list three to five possible causes from the chief complaint alone.
After the exam, rank them and write one finding that would disprove each.
Act on the highest-risk possibility first, not the most likely one.
Document the list and the ranking so the team sees your reasoning.
Review one miss per week and add the lesson to your pocket card.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: this habit sharpens your thinking; it never authorizes diagnosing or treating beyond your license.
Do not attempt to practice medicine beyond your scope because a framework made you confident; frameworks guide, licenses authorize.
Stop and get a senior clinician's eyes on any case where your differential includes a life-threatening possibility.

title: Run a structured two-minute chart review before every patient
mechanism_check: Most clinical surprises are in the chart already; the failure is reading under time pressure without a scan pattern.
A fixed scan order (allergies, meds, history, vitals trend, last note) beats reading top to bottom because critical fields get checked first every time.
Two minutes of review prevents twenty minutes of backtracking mid-visit.
improvised_tools: A five-field scan checklist: allergies, medications, key history, vital trends, last visit note.
A sticky note or margin line for the one question the chart must answer today.
A timer habit: two minutes, then you walk in, chart reviewed or not.
steps: Open the chart and scan allergies first, then active medications.
Skim key history and the last visit note for unresolved threads.
Check the vital-sign trend line, not just the latest numbers.
Write down your single must-answer question for this visit.
Walk in with the question; verify the rest with the patient directly.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: chart review prepares you; it never replaces asking the patient and examining them yourself.
Do not attempt to diagnose or prescribe from the chart alone without seeing the patient.
Stop and flag for a clinician when the chart shows allergy conflicts, dangerous interactions, or missing critical results.

title: Drill one procedural skill weekly on trainers
mechanism_check: Procedural skill decays without practice and returns fastest through short, frequent, feedback-rich repetition on a trainer.
Deliberate practice works by isolating the weakest step and repeating it with correction, not by running the whole procedure on autopilot.
Thirty focused minutes weekly preserves more skill than one annual marathon session.
improvised_tools: Any trainer on hand: manikin parts, task trainers, or improvised phantoms from clinic materials.
A checklist of the procedure's critical steps to score yourself against.
A peer or phone camera for feedback on technique.
steps: Pick this week's single skill and its critical-step checklist.
Run the procedure on the trainer slowly, narrating each step aloud.
Identify the weakest step and repeat just that step five times.
Score yourself against the checklist and note the score in a log.
Rotate skills weekly so the whole set gets touched monthly.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: trainer practice builds readiness; it never qualifies you to perform procedures beyond your license on real patients.
Do not attempt to practice invasive procedures on people outside supervised clinical training.
Stop the drill and review fundamentals if your scores trend down instead of up.

title: Use teach-back for patient instructions that stick
mechanism_check: Patients forget most of what they hear in clinic; teach-back transfers responsibility for understanding from the patient's memory to your verification loop.
The mechanism is simple: ask the patient to explain the plan in their own words, and whatever they get wrong reveals what you taught badly.
Combining clear instruction with verification catches misunderstanding while the patient is still in front of you, not at the pharmacy.
improvised_tools: Plain language and the teach-back phrase: 'I want to be sure I explained well; tell me how you'll take this.'
A written take-home sheet in the patient's language for the plan.
A circle-back question at the next visit to check retention.
steps: Give the instruction in short plain sentences, three points maximum.
Ask the patient to repeat the plan back in their own words.
Correct gently what they miss and re-explain only the missed part.
Hand over the written sheet and point to each step as you summarize.
Note in the chart that teach-back was used and what was verified.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: teach-back improves communication; it never replaces professional clinical instructions or prescribed treatment plans.
Do not attempt to give medical advice beyond your scope and training.
Stop and get help if the patient cannot understand or safely carry out the plan after two re-explanations.

title: Combine history, exam, and vitals into a one-line clinical picture
mechanism_check: A one-line synthesis forces the brain to choose what matters; the discipline of compression is what builds clinical judgment.
The classic frame is: who the patient is, the key problem, the most telling finding, and the working assessment, in a single sentence.
Combining the three data streams on paper exposes contradictions that any single stream would hide.
improvised_tools: The one-sentence template: age and key context, chief problem, standout finding, working assessment.
A scrap of paper to draft the line before presenting to a senior.
Feedback from the senior on what your line missed versus theirs.
steps: Gather the three streams: history highlights, exam standouts, vital trends.
Draft the single sentence using the template.
Check it against your differential: does the line support or contradict the top possibility?
Present the line first when asking a senior for input, then the details.
Refine the template monthly as your judgment sharpens.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: your synthesis is a communication tool for licensed clinicians to act on, not a diagnosis that authorizes treatment.
Do not attempt to act on your one-line picture beyond your licensed role.
Stop and hand the raw findings to a clinician immediately when the picture suggests a deteriorating patient.

title: Reconcile medications with a paper list and no pharmacy tech
mechanism_check: Medication errors hide in the gap between what the patient takes and what the chart says; reconciliation closes that gap by comparing sources.
The failure mode is trusting one source; the fix is three: the patient's bag, the chart list, and the patient's own words.
Discrepancies found at reconciliation are caught errors, and each caught error is a harm prevented.
improvised_tools: A paper medication list template: name, dose, frequency, last taken, source.
The patient's own pill bottles or a photo of them.
A highlighter for discrepancies between the chart and the patient.
steps: Ask the patient to bring every bottle or photograph every label.
List what the patient actually takes, including dose and timing, on the paper template.
Compare against the chart list and highlight every mismatch.
Clarify each mismatch with the patient: stopped, forgotten, or never started.
Hand the reconciled list to the prescribing clinician for correction.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: reconciliation finds discrepancies; only a licensed prescriber resolves them.
Do not attempt to advise the patient to start, stop, or change any medication yourself.
Stop and escalate urgently if you find duplicate therapy, a dangerous interaction, or an allergy conflict.

title: Mentor a junior through watch-one, do-one, teach-one
mechanism_check: Skill transfers in stages: observation builds the mental model, supervised doing builds the hands, teaching builds the understanding.
The ladder works because each stage adds a layer of ownership; skipping a rung produces fragile confidence.
Mentoring is also how the mentor audits their own habits: explaining a step forces you to notice when you have been doing it sloppily.
improvised_tools: A written ladder for each skill: watch, do supervised, do with backup, teach.
A sign-off sheet with observable criteria for each rung, not vibes.
Scheduled debrief time after every supervised attempt.
steps: Demonstrate the skill while narrating every decision, not just the motions.
Supervise the junior's first attempts with your hands ready and your corrections specific.
Advance the rung only when the criteria on the sign-off sheet are met.
Assign the junior to teach the next learner; coach their teaching, not just their technique.
Review the ladder monthly and tighten the criteria where near-misses appeared.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: mentoring develops skills under supervision; the mentor remains responsible for patient safety at every rung.
Do not attempt to sign off a junior on skills beyond your own competence or authorization.
Stop the supervised attempt and take over immediately if patient safety is at risk.

title: Debrief your own error with a fix-forward log
mechanism_check: Errors compound when hidden and shrink when examined; the log converts shame into data by separating what happened from who did it.
The mechanism is structured reflection: facts first, contributing factors second, one concrete fix third; blame is deliberately not a field.
Restoring confidence after an error comes from proving the fix works, not from pretending the error never happened.
improvised_tools: A private log template: what happened, contributing factors, one fix, follow-up date.
A trusted peer or mentor to review the entry and challenge the fix.
A monthly reread to check whether the fixes held.
steps: Write the facts within 24 hours: what happened, in order, without self-judgment.
List contributing factors honestly: fatigue, workload, missing info, skill gap.
Choose exactly one concrete fix you will implement this week.
Tell a trusted peer what happened and what you are changing.
Reread the entry in 30 days and record whether the fix held.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: this log is for learning; any error involving patient harm also follows your facility's incident-reporting and disclosure procedures.
Do not attempt to bury an error that harmed or could harm a patient; disclosure to the right people is mandatory.
Stop and seek support if an error is affecting your ability to work safely.

title: Prepare for a specialty certification with micro-study blocks
mechanism_check: Shift workers cannot sustain marathon study; spaced micro-blocks with active recall fit the life and the science of memory.
The mechanism is retrieval practice: testing yourself on a topic builds stronger memory than rereading notes about it.
Building the schedule around your actual shifts, not an ideal week, is what makes it survive contact with real life.
improvised_tools: A question bank or flashcard set for your certification.
Twenty-minute blocks between shifts, guarded on the calendar.
A score tracker showing which topics are weak, so study follows the data.
steps: Map the exam blueprint to topics and rate your current strength in each.
Schedule three 20-minute blocks per week, anchored to specific days.
Spend each block on questions and active recall, not passive reading.
Log scores by topic weekly and shift time toward the weakest areas.
Run a full practice exam monthly under timed conditions.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: certification study sharpens a licensed clinician; it does not authorize practicing the specialty before you are certified and credentialed.
Do not attempt to skip scope boundaries because you are studying the material.
Stop and rest when study fatigue starts degrading your clinical work; the job comes first.

title: Calibrate your clinical gestalt against an outcome log
mechanism_check: Intuition is pattern recognition trained on outcomes; without outcome feedback, gut calls drift toward whatever you remember most vividly, not what is true.
Calibration works by recording the gut call before the outcome is known, then comparing: this is the only honest way to measure your own accuracy.
The log reveals both overconfidence (gut wrong, certainty high) and underconfidence (gut right, certainty low) so you can tune both.
improvised_tools: A pocket log: case, gut call, confidence 1 to 5, actual outcome, lesson.
A weekly five-minute review comparing calls to outcomes.
A trend line of accuracy over months, not days.
steps: Record your gut assessment and confidence before results come back.
Fill in the actual outcome once known, without editing the original call.
Tag each miss: knowledge gap, bias, missing data, or bad luck.
Review monthly for patterns: which presentations fool you repeatedly.
Adjust your threshold for seeking senior input based on the data.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: calibration sharpens judgment; it never licenses independent clinical decisions beyond your role.
Do not attempt to rely on a 'calibrated gut' to override protocols or senior guidance.
Stop and get a second opinion whenever the log shows this presentation is one you miss.

title: Improvise a team simulation drill from stock and timers
mechanism_check: Teams fail under pressure at the seams between roles, not within them; simulation drills expose the seams in a safe setting.
A drill works by compressing a realistic scenario into minutes with an observer scoring communication and task completion.
Improvised drills beat expensive simulation centers on one metric: frequency, and frequency is what builds the reflexes.
improvised_tools: A written scenario card: patient story, vitals that evolve, a twist halfway through.
A timer and an observer with a scoring checklist.
Whatever equipment the clinic actually stocks, used as-is.
steps: Write the scenario card with the patient's story, evolving vitals, and one complication.
Assign roles, brief the team for two minutes, and start the timer.
Run the scenario for 10 to 15 minutes; the observer scores communication and tasks.
Debrief immediately: what worked, what broke, one fix to adopt.
Repeat monthly with a new scenario targeting the last drill's weakness.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: drills train licensed staff for their roles; they never substitute for professional training programs or certify anyone.
Do not attempt invasive or risky procedures during improvised drills outside proper training supervision.
Stop the drill if anyone is distressed and debrief the stress before the scenario.

title: Restore a rusty skill with a thirty-day refresh circuit
mechanism_check: Unused skills decay in a predictable curve; a concentrated refresh circuit rebuilds them faster than the original learning because the neural scaffold remains.
The circuit works by daily short practice with immediate feedback, escalating difficulty each week as the skill returns.
Restoring a skill you once held is legitimate and different from learning one from scratch; the circuit exploits that difference.
improvised_tools: The procedure checklist from your original training as the scoring standard.
A trainer or low-stakes practice setup for daily repetitions.
A daily score log to watch the recovery curve.
steps: Pick the single rusty skill and find its original training checklist.
Days 1 to 10: slow supervised repetitions, narrating each step.
Days 11 to 20: timed repetitions against the checklist standard.
Days 21 to 30: scenario variations that force adaptation.
Sign off only when scores meet the original standard three sessions running.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: a refresh circuit restores readiness for skills within your license; it does not authorize new scope.
Do not attempt to perform the skill on patients until you meet the original competency standard again.
Stop and seek retraining, not self-practice, if the skill does not recover by day 30.

title: Combine paper and phone into a field documentation kit
mechanism_check: Documentation fails in the field when the tool doesn't fit the environment: dead batteries kill phones, lost paper kills records; the pair covers each other's failure modes.
Paper is the capture layer (fast, battery-free, glanceable); the phone is the backup and transmission layer (photos, copies, send-when-connected).
The kit works when one combined routine governs both, not when they are two parallel systems.
improvised_tools: A waterproof notebook with pre-printed templates for vitals, meds, and handoffs.
A phone with offline note templates matching the paper forms.
A zip bag to protect the paper and a routine to photograph every page at shift end.
steps: Build one template set that works on paper and mirrors on the phone.
Capture on paper during the shift; it is faster and never dies.
Photograph each page at shift end into the phone as the backup copy.
Transcribe to the official record at the first connected moment.
Audit weekly: are both layers complete, or is one drifting?
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: this kit supports clinical documentation; it does not change what must be charted by licensed staff under facility policy.
Do not attempt to store identifiable patient data on personal devices in violation of privacy rules.
Stop using the kit and switch to the official system the moment it is available and reliable.

title: Improve diagnostic accuracy with a second-opinion habit
mechanism_check: A second mind breaks anchoring and availability bias; the gain comes from genuine independence of judgment before discussion, not from rubber-stamping.
Combining two independent assessments catches what one misses because errors are rarely correlated across clinicians.
The habit works when seeking input is routine and blameless, not a signal of weakness or a last resort.
improvised_tools: A standing agreement with a peer: either of us can call a two-minute case review anytime.
The one-line clinical picture format so the consult is fast and structured.
A log of consults and whether they changed the plan, to prove the habit's value.
steps: Form your independent assessment before consulting, never after.
Present the one-line picture and ask for the peer's independent take first.
Compare, discuss discrepancies, and decide together.
Log the consult: did it change the plan, and what did you learn.
Make the ask routine by doing it for straightforward cases too, not just hard ones.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: peer consults sharpen decisions among licensed staff; they never replace required physician oversight or specialist referral.
Do not attempt to use a peer's agreement to justify acting beyond your scope.
Stop and escalate to a senior clinician when the two opinions disagree on a high-stakes case.

title: Run a three-minute shift huddle: plan, risks, roles
mechanism_check: Teams drift when each member holds a different mental model of the shift; a three-minute huddle aligns everyone on the same plan before the work starts.
The mechanism is shared cognition: naming the risky patients, the thin spots, and who covers what turns implicit assumptions into explicit agreements.
Huddles work because they are short, standing, and always happen; length and irregularity are what kill them.
improvised_tools: A whiteboard or paper sheet with three columns: today's plan, watch-list patients, who covers what.
A fixed time and place that the whole team can reach in two minutes.
A timer habit: three minutes, then everyone moves.
steps: Gather the team at the fixed spot at shift start.
Name the plan: census, admissions expected, procedures scheduled.
Name the risks: watch-list patients and any staffing gaps.
Name the roles: who covers what and who is the escalation point.
End on time and post the board where the team can see it all shift.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: the huddle organizes licensed care; it never authorizes care decisions beyond each member's scope.
Do not attempt to use the huddle to bypass required physician orders or clinical protocols.
Stop and redesign the huddle if it routinely exceeds five minutes; a long huddle dies.

title: Hand off patients with SBAR so nothing gets lost
mechanism_check: Handoffs lose information because the sender knows the context and the receiver doesn't; a fixed structure forces the context across.
SBAR works by ordering the message the way a brain decides: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation, so the receiver can act on the last line.
Combining verbal SBAR with a written summary covers both ears and eyes, the two channels where handoff loss happens.
improvised_tools: The SBAR script on a pocket card until the team knows it by heart.
A written handoff sheet with the same four headings for the receiving nurse or clinician.
A read-back rule: the receiver repeats the recommendation to confirm.
steps: Prepare the SBAR before approaching the receiver: one line per letter.
Deliver it in order without skipping the Background, where most losses hide.
End with a clear Recommendation: what you need from the receiver and by when.
Hand over the written sheet and invite one clarifying question.
Confirm with read-back: the receiver states the plan in their own words.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: handoff transfers responsibility between licensed caregivers; it never delegates clinical decisions to unlicensed staff.
Do not attempt a hallway verbal-only handoff for unstable or high-risk patients.
Stop and stay with the patient if the receiver cannot accept the handoff or disputes the assessment.

title: Write role cards so a small clinic team knows who does what
mechanism_check: Small teams stall when everyone waits for someone else to act; explicit roles convert diffusion of responsibility into named ownership.
A role card works by listing three things: your tasks, your escalation trigger, and who you hand off to when you are full.
The cards are built for the busiest hour, not the average one; calm-day staffing is a different problem.
improvised_tools: Index cards or a single posted sheet with one role per section.
The three-line format per role: tasks, escalate-when, hand-off-to.
A review habit: update the cards whenever the team or the census changes.
steps: List the recurring busy-hour tasks the team actually performs.
Assign each task to a named role, with no task owned by two roles.
Write each card: tasks, the trigger that sends you for help, your relief person.
Post the sheet and walk the team through it once.
Review and revise the cards monthly or after any staffing change.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: role cards organize work within each member's licensed scope; they never assign clinical tasks to unlicensed or untrained staff.
Do not attempt to stretch one role card to cover two people's work indefinitely; understaffing is an escalation to management.
Stop and reassign immediately if a role card asks someone to work beyond their competence.

title: Drill closed-loop communication for the whole team
mechanism_check: Verbal orders get lost in noise and assumption; closed-loop communication verifies receipt by making the receiver repeat back the order.
The loop has three beats: call-out, check-back, confirm; skipping any beat reopens the gap the loop was built to close.
It works as a team drill because the failure it prevents is social (not wanting to seem slow), not technical.
improvised_tools: A posted three-beat script: 'I need X' / 'Doing X' / 'X done'.
An observer checklist for drills: did every order close the loop?
Real shift moments to practice, not just drill sessions.
steps: Teach the three beats with one demonstration the whole team watches.
Run a five-minute drill: the leader calls out orders, the team closes every loop.
Score it: count the orders that skipped a beat and name them in debrief.
Require closed-loop for all verbal orders on real shifts starting that day.
Audit weekly for a month, then fold it into orientation for new staff.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: closed-loop is a communication discipline; it never changes who is authorized to give or receive clinical orders.
Do not attempt closed-loop as a substitute for written orders where policy requires them.
Stop and clarify in writing whenever a verbal order's check-back reveals a mismatch.

title: Improvise team roles when the shift is short-staffed
mechanism_check: Short-staffing breaks teams by overload, not by missing bodies: the fix is shedding low-value work and combining roles, not heroic overtime.
The minimum viable crew keeps three functions alive: direct patient care, communication and documentation, and escalation watch.
Improvised roles work when they are named, time-boxed to the shift, and explicitly temporary.
improvised_tools: A whiteboard listing today's combined roles and who holds each.
A shed list: which non-urgent tasks are officially dropped this shift.
A relief rotation so nobody holds two roles for the whole shift.
steps: Name the three functions and assign each to a present team member.
Write the shed list and get agreement that those tasks wait.
Combine support tasks into one runner role that rotates.
Set a hard relief rotation: no one doubles up for more than two hours.
Report the shortfall upward; improvised staffing is a bridge, not a plan.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: short-staffing that endangers patients is a management and safety escalation, not a teamwork puzzle to absorb quietly.
Do not attempt to assign clinical tasks to staff outside their license or training to cover gaps.
Stop and call for emergency coverage when patient safety cannot be maintained with the crew on hand.

title: Do bedside handoff with the patient in the loop
mechanism_check: Bedside handoff works because the patient is the one witness who has been present for everything; they correct what two charts get wrong.
The mechanism is triple verification: outgoing nurse, incoming nurse, and patient all align on the plan at once.
Privacy is the design constraint, not the excuse: sensitive items move to the hallway, everything else happens at the bedside.
improvised_tools: The SBAR structure adapted to plain language for the patient's ears.
A bedside checklist: introduce, review, invite questions, confirm plan.
A privacy rule the team agrees on: what stays at the bedside, what moves.
steps: Introduce the incoming nurse to the patient by name.
Review the situation and plan in plain language the patient can follow.
Invite the patient to add or correct anything.
Confirm the next steps and who to call for what.
Move sensitive topics to the hallway, then return to confirm.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: bedside handoff improves transfer between licensed caregivers; it never replaces clinical assessment by the incoming clinician.
Do not attempt bedside handoff for patients who cannot consent or are in acute distress without adapting.
Stop and use a private handoff when the patient declines or privacy cannot be protected.

title: Debrief the shift with a five-minute plus-delta round
mechanism_check: Teams repeat the same friction when nobody names it; a five-minute debrief converts the day's friction into tomorrow's fix.
Plus-delta works by separating what to keep from what to change, which keeps the conversation forward-looking instead of blaming.
The round restores morale because ending the shift on an acknowledged win counteracts the negativity bias of hard days.
improvised_tools: A standing five-minute slot at shift end and a facilitator who keeps it moving.
A notebook page: date, plus items, delta items, one owner for tomorrow's fix.
A follow-through habit: yesterday's delta owner reports in under a minute.
steps: Gather the team for five minutes at shift end.
Go around: each person names one plus (keep doing) and one delta (change).
Pick the single most important delta and assign it one owner.
Record it in the notebook with the date.
Open tomorrow's round by asking the owner what happened with yesterday's fix.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: debriefs improve teamwork; serious incidents and patient harm follow formal incident reporting, not just the plus-delta.
Do not attempt to use the debrief to assign blame; blame kills the honesty the round needs.
Stop the round at five minutes; an overrun debrief becomes a meeting people dread.

title: Cross-train the front desk on clinical support tasks
mechanism_check: Front-desk staff are the team's slack capacity: trained on support tasks, they absorb surge; untrained, they watch the team drown.
Cross-training works by giving non-clinical staff a bounded, rehearsed set of clinical support tasks: rooming, vitals, restocking, escorting.
The boundary is the mechanism's safety: support tasks only, with a written list of what is in and what is out.
improvised_tools: A written task list: the support tasks cross-trained staff may perform.
A buddy system: each cross-trained person shadows a clinician for two weeks.
A competency sign-off sheet with observable criteria per task.
steps: Define the bounded task list with clinical leadership and put the exclusions in writing.
Pair each trainee with a buddy clinician for supervised practice.
Sign off each task against observable criteria, never on vibes.
Put the cross-trained staff into the surge rotation explicitly.
Refresh the skills quarterly with a short skills check.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: cross-training covers support tasks only; clinical assessment and decisions stay with licensed clinicians.
Do not attempt to expand the task list under pressure beyond what was signed off.
Stop and pull the person back to front-desk duties if a task is performed unsafely.

title: Build an escalation ladder the team will actually climb
mechanism_check: Escalation fails when the trigger is vague ('if you are worried'); it works when the trigger is observable ('respiratory rate over 28, call the charge nurse').
The ladder's mechanism is graded response: each rung names who, how, and what changes when you pull it, so calling feels routine instead of dramatic.
A ladder nobody practices is decoration; the drill is what makes the first real pull fast.
improvised_tools: A posted ladder: rung, trigger, who to call, how (phone, page, in person).
Observable trigger criteria per rung, written in numbers and signs.
A quarterly drill where the team walks the ladder without a real emergency.
steps: List the situations that have ever needed help, from routine to critical.
Write each rung: the observable trigger, the person, and the contact method.
Post the ladder where the team works and walk through it together.
Drill it quarterly: one scenario, timed, then debrief.
Review the ladder after every real escalation and fix what was slow.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: the ladder routes the team to professional help faster; it never replaces calling emergency services or the physician when the trigger fires.
Do not attempt to climb past a rung because the person above seems busy; the ladder exists for exactly that moment.
Stop and redesign any rung that has never been used; an unused rung is a broken rung.

title: Build a clinic on-call tree that actually gets answered
mechanism_check: On-call trees fail through stale numbers and single points of contact; a tree works when every node has a backup and every number is tested.
The mechanism is redundancy plus testing: primary, secondary, and the rule that an unanswered call rolls over in a fixed number of minutes.
A posted tree beats a digital one at 2 a.m. because it needs no login, no battery, and no search.
improvised_tools: A posted tree diagram: role, primary name and number, backup name and number.
A test-call schedule: every number gets a live test monthly.
A rollover rule: no answer in ten minutes means the next rung calls automatically.
steps: Map every role that must be reachable after hours.
Assign a primary and a backup for each role with current numbers.
Write the rollover rule and the escalation endpoint at the top of the tree.
Test every number live once a month and update the tree the same day.
Post the tree at the desk and in the break room; no digital-only copies.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: the tree reaches professional help; it never authorizes the caller to manage an emergency alone while waiting.
Do not attempt to rely on a tree that has not been tested this month.
Stop and fix the tree the day any test call fails; a dead number is a dead rung.

title: Run micro-rest rotations for night teams
mechanism_check: Fatigue degrades vigilance long before it feels dramatic; short planned rests restore more alertness than one long break at shift end.
The mechanism is strategic napping and task rotation: 20-minute rests plus switching high-vigilance tasks before error rates climb.
A rotation works when it is scheduled and protected, not when rest is 'whenever you can'.
improvised_tools: A rotation schedule: who rests, who covers, in 20 to 30 minute blocks.
A quiet corner with a reclined chair or cot for real rest.
A handoff ritual for each rotation swap so nothing drops.
steps: Build the rotation at shift start: name every rest block and its cover.
Protect the blocks: coverage is planned, not improvised mid-shift.
Use the block for real rest (eyes closed, quiet), not charting.
Swap with a two-line handoff: watch-list patients, pending tasks.
Track near-misses by hour to prove the rotation's value to leadership.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: rest rotations protect patient safety; they never reduce required staffing below safe levels.
Do not attempt to use rest rotations to justify understaffing; report unsafe staffing upward.
Stop the rotation schedule and call for relief if anyone is too impaired to work safely.

title: Start a peer skill-sharing hour for the whole team
mechanism_check: Teams get smarter when expertise circulates; a structured sharing hour combines many specialties' tricks into one room.
The mechanism is teaching as learning: the presenter deepens their own mastery while the team gains a new tool.
It works when sessions are short, practical, and peer-led; lectures from outside are a different, weaker format.
improvised_tools: A standing monthly slot and a signup sheet for presenters.
The 30-15-15 format: 30 minutes demo, 15 practice, 15 questions.
A shared folder of one-page handouts from each session.
steps: Book the monthly slot and protect it on the schedule.
Recruit presenters from the team: everyone teaches something they do well.
Run the 30-15-15 format with hands-on practice, not slides only.
File the one-page handout where the team can find it later.
Survey the team quarterly and steer topics toward the weakest skills.
stop_conditions: Call for professional help first: peer sessions share techniques among licensed staff; they never certify anyone or authorize new scope.
Do not attempt to teach procedures beyond the presenter's competence or the audience's license.
Stop and correct immediately if a session teaches an unsafe technique.
